# Overview

A pendulum's period depends on its length and on the local acceleration due
to gravity, $g$, and hardly at all on its mass. Timing a pendulum is one of
the oldest ways to measure $g$.

**Your goal is to measure the period of a pendulum at five lengths and use
the results to find $g$ with an uncertainty.**

# Safety

The bob is heavy. Keep your face out of its path, and stop it by hand only
at the end of a swing.

| Setting | Limit |
|---------|-------|
| Release angle | 10° from vertical at most |
| Bob mass | 1 kg at most on the standard clamp |

# The apparatus

A steel bob on a light string, a clamp and stand, a metre stick, and a
photogate timer.

# How it works

For small swings the period is

$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}},$$

where $L$ is the length from the pivot to the centre of the bob. Squaring
both sides gives $T^2 = (4\pi^2/g)\,L$, so a graph of $T^2$ against $L$ is a
straight line through the origin with slope $4\pi^2/g$.

```{.tikz alt="A pendulum: a bob hanging from a pivot on a string of length L, swung out by a small angle theta." desc="A pivot at the top with a string hanging from it. The string is drawn twice: once straight down (dashed), and once swung to the right by a small angle labelled theta. A filled circle, the bob, hangs at the end of the swung string. The length of the string, from the pivot to the centre of the bob, is labelled L." width="35%"}
\begin{tikzpicture}
\draw[thick] (-1,0) -- (1,0);
\draw[dashed] (0,0) -- (0,-3);
\draw (0,0) -- ({3*sin(15)},{-3*cos(15)}) node[midway, right] {$L$};
\fill ({3*sin(15)},{-3*cos(15)}) circle (0.18);
\draw (0,-0.9) arc (-90:-75:0.9) node[midway, below] {$\theta$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

# Setup

| From | To |
|------|----|
| Photogate signal lead | Timer input A |
| Timer power lead | Bench outlet |

# Procedure

1. Set the length $L$ to about 1.0 m and measure it from the pivot to the
   centre of the bob.
2. Pull the bob aside by no more than 10° and release it without a push.
3. Record the time for 10 full swings. Repeat three times.
4. Repeat steps 1 to 3 for four shorter lengths, down to about 0.3 m.

| Length $L$ (m) | Time for 10 swings (s) | Period $T$ (s) |
|----------------|------------------------|----------------|
| (your value)   | (your value)           | (your value)   |

# Analysis questions

1. Plot $T^2$ against $L$ and fit a straight line. What is $g$, with its
   uncertainty?
2. Does your line pass through the origin? What would an offset mean?

# Sources

These instructions are an original example written for the toolkit. The
small-angle period is derived in any introductory mechanics text, for
example [Nelson and Olsson, "The pendulum: rich physics from a simple
system"](https://doi.org/10.1119/1.14703).
